seo.title: Karmic tail 9 12 12 compatibility: the climb without looking back
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 12 12 compatibility: The Hermit at the entry and two Hanged Men. Why no person has this tail, what holds the couple, how to end the suspension.

title: Karmic tail 9-12-12 in compatibility: two who must not look back
short: The triple 9-12-12 cannot be found in any personal destiny matrix. To become a person's tail, it would need The Devil in the centre of the chart, and no person ever has The Devil in the centre. A couple does: 82.4% of couples with this tail. What holds these two together belongs to neither of them — it appears only between them.

sections.h2: A tail that no single person has
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the tail obeys a strict rule: the entry M is the reduced sum of the main task D and the centre of the chart. If the task is 12 and the entry is 9, the centre has to be 15: 12 + 15 = 27, 2 + 7 = 9. But the centre of a personal matrix can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. Fifteen never appears there, for any date of birth. So 9-12-12 is impossible as a personal tail.

In a couple's matrix every point is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's centre is built from two personal centres, and The Devil appears in the sum easily: 10 + 5, 8 + 7. Going through every date shows that 82.4% of couples with the 9-12-12 tail have exactly 15 in the centre. For them the tail is built by the law of a personal tail — only the missing card comes not from one person but from two. The remaining 17.6% have The Lovers (6) in the centre.

The middle is not personal either. In a personal chart the middle of the tail comes from its two ends, and 9 + 12 would give 21, The World. A couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles, and it comes out as 12. That is why the triple 9-12-12 appears nowhere in a personal chart: not in the tail, and not on the money, relationship or talent lines, where the middle number is also always the sum of the outer two. Whoever sees these three numbers is looking at a couple's matrix.
The tail is not rare: about one couple in 42 has it (2.389%), the 13th most common of the 97 couple tails.

The arithmetic can be read as an image. For most of these couples the entry is the sum of the main task and the centre: The Hermit is The Hanged Man plus The Devil. **This couple's silence is made of suspension and attachment** — an attachment so strong that a careless word feels dangerous. This is our reading, not a rule of the method, but the numbers suggest it on their own.

The marriage of Orpheus and Eurydice in Ovid's Metamorphoses (Books X and XI) lasts a few lines. Hymen, the god of weddings, comes to the feast, but without songs or good omens. Soon the bride dies of a snakebite. Orpheus goes down to the underworld and sings before its rulers, Persephone and her husband. The song is so beautiful that they let Eurydice go on one condition: Orpheus must not turn round until he has left the valleys of Avernus. The two climb in silence. Near the very edge he looks back, and she vanishes a second time.

This story holds everything the 9-12-12 tail is made of. Two people walk one behind the other in silence, each alone with their own thoughts — The Hermit. The whole road rests on a condition and on waiting — The Hanged Man. The main trial is to hold on without checking — The Hanged Man again. And between them lies the strongest attachment and a fear of loss that rises right at the threshold — The Devil in the centre.

The myth is not a prediction. Ovid and Virgil end it in grief, Gluck's opera of 1762 ends it happily, and Ovid himself gives one more ending in the following book. The tail shows which scene keeps repeating in a couple, but not how it will end. Nor are its roles tied to gender: either of the two may walk in front.

sections.h2: A wedding without words: The Hermit at the entry
paragraphs: Ovid begins this love story with silence. Here is Hymen at the wedding, in Brookes More's translation:

Truly Hymen there / was present during the festivities / of Orpheus and Eurydice, but gave / no happy omen, neither hallowed words / nor joyful glances; and the torch he held / would only sputter, fill the eyes with smoke, / and cause no blaze while waving.

There is light, but it will not blaze, and no solemn words are spoken. For the 9-12-12 tail this is an exact image of the entry: the fire is already burning, quietly and low, and words seem unnecessary.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: its shared wishes and common language. With The Hermit on this point, both want the same thing — a world of their own where nothing has to be proved. Love is shown by deeds: meeting the six o'clock train, fixing the tap without a word, buying that particular book. Friends hear about important things once everything is already decided. Each has their own time and their own corner, and that is respected. No step is rushed — not the first confession, not moving in, not the wedding.

Benebell Wen offers two readings of The Hermit's lantern. The first is the familiar one: a light in the darkness for others. The second fits this entry better: someone "who sees the world through his or her own light", who "walks in the direction of his own thoughts only". At the 9-12-12 entry each partner carries their own lantern and sees the other by its light — as the other appears to them.

In Virgil's Georgics, Orpheus after his loss sings of his wife like this: "you, sweet wife, you he sang, alone with himself on the lonely shore, you as the day came, you as it went" (our translation). This is The Hermit's love in its purest form: a conversation with the other that goes on inside oneself.

The entry stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish turns into resistance. "We understand each other anyway" turns into "we don't talk about that". Questions pile up in silence, each lives in a room of their own, and one day it turns out that the two have long been walking side by side without seeing each other. From outside such a couple can look cold, even though inside something is burning — like Hymen's torch, which smokes but does not go out.

sections.h2: The climb in silence: The Hanged Man in the middle
paragraphs: Ovid describes the condition and the road in a few lines; in Brookes More's translation:

Pluto told him he / might now ascend from these Avernian vales / up to the light, with his Eurydice; / but, if he turned his eyes to look at her, / the gift of her delivery would be lost. / They picked their way in silence up a steep / and gloomy path of darkness.

The middle of the task is how the couple walks from the wish to the main task. With The Hanged Man here, the path runs through suspension. On this path Eurydice is no longer dead and not yet alive; in Ovid she walks "with slow steps, yet halting from her wound". Orpheus has found her and has not: she is one step behind, but he may not see her. Waite writes of The Hanged Man: "life in suspension, but life and not death". Eurydice's climb is that kind of life, literally.

In a couple's life the middle 12 looks like this. The big decision waits "for better times": moving in after the renovation, marrying once things settle at work, having the talk when the right moment comes. One leads — knows where and why — and the other follows without knowing the plan. The one in front does not look back and does not explain, believing that this is how it must be, that it is safer. The one behind keeps quiet so as not to get in the way. Sometimes only a push from outside can move the couple — news, a move, someone else's wedding.

This middle has a strong side too. The Hanged Man knows how to wait and how to see a situation from the other side. Such couples sense each other at a distance, give way without keeping score, and do a great deal for each other in silence. One of the card's messages, in Wen's words, is to "hang in there": suspension can be endured. The question is whether it ends.

sections.h2: The backward glance: The Hanged Man in the main task
paragraphs: Here are the lines on which the whole myth rests, in Brookes More's translation:
in fear he might again / lose her, and anxious for another look / at her, he turned his eyes so he could gaze / upon her. Instantly she slipped away.

There are two motives, named outright: fear and longing. Not indifference and not betrayal — Ovid calls Orpheus amans, "the lover", at that very moment (flexit amans oculos, "the lover turned his eyes"). Orpheus looked back to make sure she was there. The main task of the tail is read mostly through its minus, and the minus of The Hanged Man here is not the sacrifice itself but the fact that the sacrifice cannot bear the silence and breaks into checking.

Russian has a word for this — oglyadka, "a backward glance". Zhit' s oglyadkoy, "to live with a backward glance", means to be over-careful and keep checking: is it still there, have we lost it, what will people say. Lyubit' bez oglyadki, "to love without a backward glance", means to give oneself completely. **A couple with the 9-12-12 tail wants the second and lives the first.** In Waite's divinatory lists, both The Hermit and The Hanged Man carry the word circumspection, from the Latin circumspicere, "to look around". In the 9-12-12 tail that circumspection is written three times.

What the backward glance looks like in a couple. Every evening one asks: "Are you sure you're not upset? Are we really all right?" The other says "yes" and feels checked up on. Decisions are made "the proper way", with one eye on the family: what the parents will think, how it looks from outside. The picture outside is flawless; inside are two people trying very hard and very tired. One of them holds everything together with all their strength and hears reproaches in return. They cannot leave, and they cannot explain either.
Three authors told this scene in different ways, and together they show how the main task unfolds.
In Ovid, Eurydice does not reproach him: "what had she to complain of — his great love?"

In the fourth book of Virgil's Georgics she cries out: "Who has ruined both poor me and you, Orpheus? What madness is this?" Virgil himself calls the act "a sudden madness", one "to be forgiven, if the dead knew how to forgive". Then Orpheus clutches at shadows and wants "to say many things" — but there is no one left to say them to (our translations).

In Gluck — the opera Orfeo ed Euridice, Vienna, 1762, libretto by Ranieri de' Calzabigi — the twist is the most exact. Eurydice does not know the condition. Love tells Orpheus: "Gli sguardi trattieni, affrena gli accenti" — "hold back your glances, rein in your words". She walks behind a husband who will not look at her and will not say why. She begs for a single glance, calls him faithless and a tyrant, says that death is dearer to her than life with him. He answers: "Ben potrò morir d'affanno, ma giammai dirò perché" — "I may well die of grief, but I will never say why." She asks: "What secret is Orpheus hiding from me?" — and weeps that he has abandoned her. And Orpheus turns round: not from his own fear, but from her pain (our translations).

This is the mechanism of the 9-12-12 main task. One keeps silent for the sake of the couple and is sure this is a sacrifice. The other sees only the silence and reads it as coldness or betrayal. In Waite's list for The Hermit, "treason" and "dissimulation" stand right next to "prudence": "Prudence, circumspection; also and especially treason, dissimulation". Prudent silence from inside and betrayal from outside are one and the same silence, seen from two sides. The longer the condition lasts, the louder the reproach, and the more certain it is that someone will turn round — not because they have stopped loving, but because they can bear no more.

So the couple's task is not to endure even more: The Hanged Man is not just patience. The task is to **say the condition out loud**. "I can't explain right now — and here is why." "I'm putting this off until spring, not for ever." "I'm afraid you'll fall behind, so I keep looking back." A condition that has been spoken stops being a secret, and so it stops working as a wall.

sections.h2: Seven days on the bank: when suspension becomes a home
paragraphs: After the second loss Orpheus tries to go back for Eurydice, but the ferryman will not let him across. In Brookes More's translation:
Seven days he sat upon Death's river bank, / in squalid misery and without all food — / nourished by grief, anxiety, and tears — / complaining that the Gods of Erebus / were pitiless.

Orpheus cannot go back and cannot leave. He sits by the river, feeds on grief and blames his misfortune on the "pitiless" gods, and then for three years he shuns everyone. The suspension that used to be a road becomes a home.

In couples with this tail it can happen quietly. After a failed attempt — a move that fell through, a talk that ended in a quarrel — the couple stops trying. Circumstances are to blame, or work, or parents, or "fate". Each goes back to their own lantern, and everything returns to the entry: silence, only now with more hurt in it. That is how the tail closes into a circle — The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Hanged Man, and The Hermit again.

sections.h2: The Dweller on the Threshold: the couple's centre in Waite and Wen
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In 82.4% of couples with the 9-12-12 tail, The Devil sits there.

In The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Waite says that what this card signifies is "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit". The figure of the Dweller on the Threshold came into occult writing from Bulwer-Lytton's novel Zanoni (1842). Orpheus loses exactly at the threshold: in Ovid there remained "but little more to climb till they would touch earth's surface"; in Virgil it happens "right at the edge of the light". The Devil in these couples' centre is what rises at the threshold: when almost everything has worked out, the fear of losing grows stronger than trust.

Wen opens her description of The Devil on the Waite–Smith card like this: "The Lovers from Key 6 are chained by a horned beast". So the centre of 9-12-12 couples holds either The Lovers (17.6%) or the same Lovers in chains (82.4%). Wen also links The Devil with Mara, the tempter of the Buddha, who personifies "the thirst for existence, the thirst for pleasure, the thirst for power". In Ovid, Orpheus turns round avidus videndi, "greedy to see".

In its plus, The Devil in a couple's atmosphere is strong attraction, passion and a rare acceptance: here no one has to hide their dark side, and mistakes are forgiven. In its minus it is the wish to possess, jealousy, control and silence about one's own desires. Together with The Hermit's silence at the entry this is a risky mix: desires go unspoken, while the two hold on to each other very tightly. Waite leaves hope in the description of the card itself: the one who is exalted over the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever".

Orpheus himself speaks the key to this centre when he pleads with the rulers of the underworld. Brookes More renders it as "I ask of you / possession of her few days as a boon". The Latin is sharper: pro munere poscimus usum — "I ask not for a gift, but for a loan" (our translation). A beloved person cannot be owned; one can only walk beside them. In her advice to couples with energy 15, Yuliana Lisovskaya reaches the same thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

sections.h2: What such a couple is made of
paragraphs: A couple's tail is the sum of the partners' personal tails, and for 9-12-12 there are only three combinations.

ul: **12-19-7 + 15-20-5 — 78% of these couples.** One partner's personal tail begins with The Hanged Man, the other's with The Devil. In the couple these two cards go deeper: The Hanged Man becomes the main task, The Devil the centre. The middle is the sum of The Sun and Judgement, cards of clarity and awakening: 19 + 20 = 39 → 12. Two bright lights add up to suspension.

**18-6-6 + 18-6-6 — 18%.** Both have the same personal tail, and both have The Hanged Man in the centre of their personal chart. In the couple the cards swap places: The Lovers from the two personal tails give the Hanged Men of the couple's tail, and the two Hanged Men from the personal centres give The Lovers in the couple's centre.

**3-7-22 + 6-5-17 — 4%.** The Empress and The Lovers at the entries give The Hermit, The Chariot and The Hierophant give The Hanged Man in the middle, The Fool and The Star give The Hanged Man in the task.

paragraphs: None of these five personal tails contains The Hermit. **Neither partner brings the silence at the entry with them — it is born between them.** The numbers cannot say who is "to blame" for the silence or for the backward glance: both are made by two.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a second Hermit or The Moon
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together. In 65.7% of couples with the 9-12-12 tail this is The Hermit again; in 34.3% it is The Moon.

The second Hermit changes the meaning of the first. At the entry silence hides; in the values it deepens: conversations after which something changes, respect for the other's quiet, the ability to learn from each other. The lantern each carried for themselves becomes a light in which both can be seen.

The Moon in the values is a path through the dark, where trust has to rest not on the eyes but on feeling. This is exactly what Orpheus's climb teaches: to walk without seeing the other, and to know that they are there.

The person born on 17.01.1976 has the personal tail 15-20-5 and The Wheel of Fortune (10) in the centre. The person born on 05.07.1975 has the tail 12-19-7 and The Hierophant (5) in the centre. The couple's matrix adds their points pair by pair:

The middle 12 comes from the partners' middles, not from the ends of the couple's tail: 9 + 12 would have given The World. This couple's values are The Hermit (9), and that is not the sum of the personal values either: 3 + 15 would have given The Moon, but the couple's values are recalculated from the couple's own points. In this couple The Hermit also sits on the attitude to material things (5 + 22 = 27 → 9), and in Lisovskaya, The Hermit in money means unhurried spending and something always put aside for a rainy day.

sections.h2: The way out: side by side, then each in front
paragraphs: In Book XI Ovid brings Orpheus back to Eurydice and describes how they walk now. In Brookes More's translation:
Then lovingly they wandered side by side, / or he would follow when she chose to lead, / or at another time he walked in front, / looking back, safely, — at Eurydice.

Ovid sets this scene in the fields of the blessed — a poetic convention, not a promise. But the way of walking he describes can be taken into life. It corrects both mistakes of the first climb: no one is always in front, and a look back is no longer a check.

There is a hint in the numbers too. Lisovskaya adds up repeated energies: the tail's two Hanged Men give 12 + 12 = 24 → 6. Add up the whole tail, 9 + 12 + 12 = 33 → 6 — The Lovers again. Lisovskaya herself notes that such a sum sounds faintly if its card does not appear in the matrix; in 17.6% of 9-12-12 couples The Lovers stand right in the centre. **Beneath the silence and the suspension The Lovers are hidden** — the card of choice. In Gluck the ending is brought by Love. For a 9-12-12 couple it is brought by a choice made out loud.
What this means in practice:

ul: **Name the condition.** If one partner is silently carrying something "for us", say what it is, why, and until when. Gluck's whole disaster lies in the words "I will never say why".
**Give "later" a deadline.** The Hanged Man is a pause, not a home. A postponed decision needs a date, or at least a next step.
**Change places.** Whoever is always in front should sometimes walk behind: with money, with holidays, in talks with the family. Whoever is always behind gets the right to lead.
**Ask instead of checking.** "Are you there?" asked out loud costs less than a secret backward glance, and it sounds like care rather than control.
**Don't pay with sacrifice.** Agree on what each keeps for themselves — time, money, friends — so that "everything for the other" does not turn into a silent ledger.

**Call for help when it is frightening.** If constant fear, control or pressure have settled into the couple, that is a reason to see a family psychologist. If there is danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line.

paragraphs: The strong version of the 9-12-12 tail is a couple that can be silent without fear. Its silence is trust, not a wall: each can withdraw into themselves, knowing the other will not vanish. It knows how to wait and knows what it is waiting for. And it looks at the other the way Orpheus does at the end of the myth: without fear.

ul: Ovid, Metamorphoses, X, 1–77 and XI, 61–66; translation by Brookes More (1922). The Latin words pro munere poscimus usum are X, 37; the other Latin and the English renderings of them are ours.
Gluck, Orfeo ed Euridice (1762), libretto by R. de' Calzabigi, Acts I and III; translations ours.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910): The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Devil.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Devil.
Yu. Lisovskaya, Matritsa sud'by: sovmestimost' (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and energies 9, 12, 15.

intro: The karmic tail 9-12-12 in compatibility is the task of a couple that enters the union through silence and lives in suspension. **The Hermit at the entry** is the shared wish: a quiet world for two, where words are not needed and no step is rushed. **The Hanged Man in the middle** is how the couple walks the path: postponing, waiting, with one of them silently carrying the load for both. **The Hanged Man in the main task** is what the couple has to learn: to stop paying for the union with silent sacrifice and an endless "later", to trust without checking, and to say out loud what the silence costs.

The story of these three cards is older than any matrix. Ovid wrote it down: two people climb out of the underworld in complete silence, he in front, she behind, and he must not turn round. What follows is an investigation: what the numbers themselves say, what Waite and Benebell Wen write about the cards, and why the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice fits the 9-12-12 tail so closely.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-12-12 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that enters the union through silence and lives in suspension. The Hermit at the entry is the wish for a quiet world of two. The Hanged Man in the middle is a path of waiting and silent sacrifice. The Hanged Man in the main task means learning not to pay for the union with silence, to give "later" a deadline, to trust without checking and to say out loud what the silence costs.

faq.q: Can 9-12-12 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal tail the entry equals the reduced sum of the task and the centre, so a task of 12 and an entry of 9 would need a centre of 15, which no person has. On the money, relationship and talent lines the middle number is the sum of the outer two, and 9 + 12 gives 21. The triple 9-12-12 exists only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Why does the couple tail 9-12-12 have two Hanged Men?
faq.a: The middle and the main task of the couple are built from different points of the partners: the middle from the middles of their personal tails, the task from their karmic tasks. In couples with this tail both sums reduce to 12. These are two different roles: in the middle The Hanged Man shows how the couple walks the path, in the task — what it has to learn.

faq.q: What does The Devil in the centre mean for a couple with the 9-12-12 tail?
faq.a: It sits in the centre of 82.4% of these couples and describes the atmosphere of the union: strong attraction and acceptance, but also fear of loss, the wish to possess, silence about one's own desires. No person has The Devil in the centre — this card appears only in a couple. The remaining 17.6% have The Lovers in the centre.

faq.q: Is the 9-12-12 tail a verdict on the couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict a break-up and does not say how the union will end. It shows a recurring difficulty — suspension, silent sacrifice and checking — and the direction of the work. The strong version of this tail is a couple that can be silent without fear and can wait, knowing what it is waiting for.

faq.q: Is there a couple tail 12-9-12 or 12-12-9?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these numbers appear only in the order 9-12-12, with The Hermit at the entry and two Hanged Men after it.

report: Ovid explains the most famous backward glance in literature in two words. Orpheus was leading Eurydice out of the underworld, he was forbidden to turn round, and near the very edge he turned — "in fear he might again lose her, and anxious for another look at her". Not out of indifference: Ovid calls him amans, "the lover", at that very moment. The couple tail 9-12-12 tells this story in three cards — The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Hanged Man — and shows why two people who treasure each other so much are so afraid of one careless word.

report.h3: A silence that neither of them brings

report: The Hermit at the entry is what the couple wants together: a quiet world for two, where nothing has to be proved. There is fire, there are no words, and words seem unnecessary.

The main task is The Hanged Man again, and it is read through its minus. Russian has an exact word for it: oglyadka, "a backward glance". To live with a backward glance is to keep checking: is it still there, have we lost it, what will people say. To love without a backward glance is to give oneself completely. **A couple with the 9-12-12 tail wants the second and lives the first.** Every evening one asks: "Still not upset? "I keep looking back because I'm scared of finding no one behind me."

report.h3: Not a gift, but a loan

report: Most of these couples have The Devil in the centre — a card that never appears in the centre of anyone's personal matrix. Waite calls it the Dweller on the Threshold, and Orpheus loses exactly at the threshold, when almost everything has worked out. The Devil in a couple's atmosphere is strong attraction and a rare acceptance, but also fear of loss, the wish to possess, silence about one's own desires. How people walk once this is understood, Ovid shows in the next book: "Then lovingly they wandered side by side, / or he would follow when she chose to lead, / or at another time he walked in front, / looking back, safely, — at Eurydice." unit.meaning: Your task is to stop paying for the union with silence and an endless "later": say the condition aloud, trust without checks.
